segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Hello, this is 6 Minute English from BBC Learning English. I'm Neil.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: And I'm Beth. In this programme, we're talking about politeness.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: Britain has a reputation for being a polite place where children are told to say please and thank you.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: But in real life, that isn't always true. You, give me that pen.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: I'm sorry, that was a bit rude.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: Well, what should I have said?

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: How about, Neil, please could you pass me the pen?

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: Fine. Neil, could you please pass me the pen?

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: There you go, that's much better.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: Now listen as BBC Radio 4 presenter Michael Rosen,

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: who is a well-known poet and children's author in Britain,

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: describes what happened to him one day.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: Recently, this is how it went.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: A boy was walking past me in the street,

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: stomped and said,

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: Hey, you're a thingy, innit?

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: Now, that one seems to break all the rules.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: And because it broke the rules, it gave me a problem.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: How do I answer it?

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: A boy saw Michael Rosen and said,

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: Hey, you're thingy, innit?

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: He used the word thingy because, although he recognised Michael,

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: he couldn't remember his name.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: He also said, innit, which is short for isn't it,

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: to emphasise what he'd said.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: So, was the boy being impolite,

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: or was he just happy meeting a famous person in the street?

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: And why do we teach kids to be polite in the first place That what we be discussing in this programme using some useful new vocabulary

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: But first I have a question for you Neil The British are well known for being polite

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: as we've said, and there's even an idiom we use in certain situations to remind someone

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: to be especially polite. But what is it? Is it A. Mind your A's and B's, B. Mind your

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: P's and Q's or C, mind your X's and Y's?

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Well, I know the answer to this but I'm going to say C, mind your X's and Y's because I

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: think it's brilliant.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: OK, interesting. Well, we'll find out the correct answer later in the programme. So,

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: let's return to the boy who said, hey, your thingy, innit, to famous poet Michael Rosen.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: Was that impolite or not? Professor Louise Mullaney, who studies the language of politeness,

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: has an answer. She thinks that politeness is as much to do with the person being spoken to

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: as the person speaking, as she explained to BBC Radio 4 programme Word of Mouth.

segments.speaker: Louise Mullany
segments.text: I think the crucial thing there is in how you've perceived it. So obviously he's not giving us the

segments.speaker: Louise Mullany
segments.text: conventional, oh, good afternoon, Mr. Rosen, or a more formal approach. It's very, very informal.

segments.speaker: Louise Mullany
segments.text: And he can't remember your name and he's saying in it. Now that has been interpreted by you as

segments.speaker: Louise Mullany
segments.text: non-threatening to you. You don't see him as insulting you and you're actually quite

segments.speaker: Louise Mullany
segments.text: kindly disposed to that person. So you haven't interpreted it as offensive or aggressive.

segments.speaker: Louise Mullany
segments.text: You said I think you described it as being quite civil actually

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Michael Rosen didn feel that the boy was insulting him To insult someone means to be rude or offensive to them

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: Although his speech was very informal Michael thought the boy was actually pleased to see him not rude at all

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: Michael was well disposed to the boy. He liked and approved of him.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: So, you could say that politeness is subjective.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: If Michael doesn't feel offended, then where is the offence?

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Then why do we teach children to be polite at all?

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Well, according to Professor Mullaney, it's to do with the rules of society.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: That's right. Louise thinks that by teaching our kids politeness,

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: they enjoy the benefits of being accepted in society.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: So imagine how embarrassed she felt when her two-year-old daughter

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: repeatedly ignored the cook at her nursery school and refused to say hello.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: Here's Louise Mullaney telling the story to BBC Radio 4's Word of Mouth.

segments.speaker: Louise Mullany
segments.text: The cook looks so disappointed.

segments.speaker: Louise Mullany
segments.text: And as I mention in the book, it felt to me like there were lots of other children

segments.speaker: Louise Mullany
segments.text: skipping and jumping past, going hello, being really friendly children.

segments.speaker: Louise Mullany
segments.text: And my daughter was just there and we started to make excuses for her,

segments.speaker: Louise Mullany
segments.text: like, oh, she's tired, oh, she's teething, she's this and she's that,

segments.speaker: Louise Mullany
segments.text: because the embarrassment was so strong.

segments.speaker: Louise Mullany
segments.text: And I felt awful walking back past the kitchen on my way out.

segments.speaker: Louise Mullany
segments.text: I was almost trying to hide my face, going, I'm the one with the really rude child.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: When her daughter didn't say hello to an adult, Louise made excuses for her. If you make excuses

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: for someone you try to explain the reasons for their behaviour For example Louise said her daughter was tired she was growing new teeth she was this and that The idiom this and that can be used to describe various unspecified things For example if someone asks what you did this afternoon you might reply oh not much I stayed at home I watched

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: TV, I did this and that.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: Politeness means different things to different people, but we still like it when people are

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: polite to us. And I think the polite thing to do now is reveal the answer to my question,

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: Neil. So the idiom that we use to remind someone to be polite is not mind your X's and Y's. I'm

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: sorry Neil, it's mind your P's and Q's.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: That's a shame. X's and Y's is much better.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: OK, now let's recap the vocabulary we've learnt, starting with thingy, an informal word that's used

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: if you can't remember someone's or something's name. People also use the slang words what's his

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: name or what's a name for the same reason.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: In it is a short form of the tag question, isn't it? It's used to add emphasis to a statement.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: The adjective insulting means rude or offensive.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: If you are well disposed to someone, you like and approve of them.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: When you make excuses for someone, you explain the reasons for their bad behaviour.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: And finally, the idiom this and that describes various unspecified things.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Once again, our six minutes are up, but why not test yourself with the programme quiz and worksheet available now on our website, bbclearningenglish.com.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Goodbye for now.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: Bye.
